extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors preparing/working through mathematical olympiad problems (advanced high-school/undergraduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Solved problems and worked proofs in algebra and geometry typical for mathematical olympiads: techniques for equations with radicals, recurrences, inequalities (convexity, rearrangement), Vieta/root manipulations, induction, and geometric inequality arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take conjugates to simplify radical expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: When an equation or expression involves square roots, take the conjugate (multiply numerator/denominator or apply conjugate to sum/difference of radicals) to simplify and isolate terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly (e.g., Problems 1.64, 1.65, 1.68, 1.69, 1.70) to eliminate nested radicals, obtain equivalent algebraic equations, deduce sign/domain constraints (e.g. x>0, m>0), and create expressions that telescope or lead to polynomial relations. Check resulting domain conditions after squaring to avoid extraneous solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive and use domain/positivity constraints before algebraic manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify necessary domain conditions (like x>0, radicands nonnegative, parameters positive) before proceeding with algebraic transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in radical equations note x must be positive; deduce m must be positive. Use these to justify squaring or dividing by expressions that must be nonzero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form linear recurrences from conjugate-symmetric expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Express quantities as sum of conjugate algebraic numbers (e.g., (a + b√c)^k + (a - b√c)^k) to obtain integer sequences satisfying linear recurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Problem 1.65: x_k = (5 - 2√6)^k + (5 + 2√6)^k satisfies x_{k+2} = 10 x_{k+1} - x_k. Such recurrences give integrality and congruence properties via induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurrence relations + induction to prove integrality and congruences
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a recurrence with integer initial terms is found, prove by induction that all terms are integers and satisfy congruence properties (e.g., x_k ≡ 2 (mod 4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show base cases and propagation using the recurrence; use congruence arithmetic to deduce divisibility properties for constructed integers (e.g., nk = (xk + 2)/4 integer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain lower/upper bounds by rewriting with conjugates and integer numerators
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite expressions involving roots by taking conjugates to isolate an integer numerator (e.g., |2a^2 - 3b^2|) over algebraic denominators, then use integrality/nonzero to produce explicit numeric bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.66: recognizing numerator is nonzero integer gives |numerator| ≥ 1, control denominator via variable bounds to get explicit lower bound (≥ 1/350).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create telescoping sums via algebraic factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulate terms (often radicals) into differences of successive terms so that when summed the series telescopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Problems 1.68, 1.69, 1.70: rewrite each term as sqrt(A_n) - sqrt(A_{n-1}) or similar so partial sums collapse to a small expression; often requires factorization or conjugate manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use convexity/concavity and Jensen-type arguments for inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a function f whose convexity or concavity (via second derivative sign) applies; then use f(a)+f(b) ≥ 2f((a+b)/2) (or reverse) or weighted versions to derive inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: f(x)=x^n convex → (a^n + b^n)/2 ≥ ((a+b)/2)^n (Problem 1.74); f(x)=log x concave → AM-GM via Jensen (Problem 1.76); choose appropriate f for the structure of the inequality and justify convexity by f''(x)>0 (or <0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use weighted concavity/convexity with chosen weights to exploit sum constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Select weights λ_i summing to 1 to apply concavity/convexity so that a weighted sum of f(x_i) is bounded by f(weighted average).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.79: choose λ1=1/10, λ2=2/10, λ3=3/10, λ4=4/10 to bound sum of square roots given constraints on partial sums; combine with linear bounds to finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove inequalities by induction with a strengthened hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving an inequality inductively, prove a stronger statement which makes induction straightforward (e.g., multiply by next factor and show needed relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.83: prove a stronger inequality involving a multiplicative correction term 1 - 1/2^n to facilitate induction from n to n+1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ordering/WLOG assumptions to apply monotone inequality tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume variables are ordered (e.g., a ≤ b ≤ c) without loss of generality to compare monotone sequences (a^k, b^k, etc.) and apply rearrangement or Chebyshev inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently used before applying rearrangement (Problems 1.108–1.113) or to compare signs of differences (Problem 1.76). Justify WLOG via symmetry or cyclicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the rearrangement inequality by matching monotone sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: For ordered sequences a1 ≤ ... ≤ an and b1 ≤ ... ≤ bn, the maximal (resp. minimal) sum of products is achieved by similarly (resp. oppositely) ordered pairings; compare given sum to rearranged sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 1.108–1.113: use rearrangement to lower-bound or upper-bound cyclic sums by pairing variables in sorted order or summing cyclic shifts to derive Chebyshev and related inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive Chebyshev by summing rearrangements over cyclic shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sum multiple rearrangement inequalities (over cyclic permutations of the b-sequence) and factor to obtain Chebyshev: (mean a)(mean b) ≤ mean(ab).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.112: add n rearrangement inequalities and divide by n to reach Chebyshev's inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pairwise swap (inversion) argument to minimize/maximize symmetric products
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that swapping two misordered pairings (an inversion) reduces (or increases) the product/sum, so the global minimum/maximum is reached when sequences are similarly ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.113: swapping bσ(i) and bσ(j) when σ(i)>σ(j) reduces the product; repeat until sorted, proving (a1+b1)... minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite cyclic inequalities into symmetric form and clear denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply through to eliminate denominators, collect like terms, and reduce the cyclic inequality to an equivalent symmetric polynomial inequality where rearrangement or ordering can be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.111: clear denominators to obtain a3b3 + b3c3 + c3a3 ≥ a2bc3 + b2ca3 + c2ab3, then assume ordering and apply rearrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Viète's relations to translate between symmetric sums and polynomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For polynomial with roots x_i, use sums/products of roots in terms of coefficients to set up equations, factor polynomials, or derive relations between roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple problems (1.95–1.102, 1.97–1.100) use Viète to deduce coefficients given symmetric conditions, to build auxiliary polynomials, or to transform expressions into polynomial identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform roots via rational functions to find new polynomial for transformed roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Given roots x_k and a transform y_k = g(x_k) (e.g., y_k = 1/(1-x_k)), derive the polynomial with roots y_k and apply Viète to compute sums/products of y_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.99: set y_k = 1/(1-x_k), substitute into the original root equation, clear denominators to get polynomial P(y) whose coefficients give y1+...+yn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encode power sums Sn = x^n + y^n + z^n via linear recurrences from polynomial relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If x,y,z are roots of t^3 + bt + c = 0, then power sums satisfy linear recurrences Sn+3 + b Sn+1 + c Sn = 0; use initial Sn to solve for coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.101: use the recurrence Sn+3 + b Sn+1 - 6 Sn = 0 with given S3 and S7 to solve for b and obtain roots; this technique encodes symmetric power sums into linear relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor a quartic as product of quadratics to match system-of-equations structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when a system of symmetric equations corresponds to coefficients of product of quadratics; factor the quartic and read off coefficients to find variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.102: identify x^4 + 8x^3 + 23x^2 + 28x + 12 as product of two monic quadratics; compare to x^2 + ax + c times x^2 + bx + d to recover a,b,c,d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check monotonicity via derivative sign to locate roots in intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute derivative f' and its sign on intervals to determine where f is increasing/decreasing; combine with endpoint values to show existence/number of real roots in specified intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.96: f'(x)=3x^2-4x+1 analysis shows monotonicity on subintervals and uses endpoint values f(0)=p, f(1/3)=p+4/27, f(1)=p to deduce real roots' locations and constraints on p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraic identities to produce factorizations that reveal prime/divisor structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply identities (e.g., x^2 - x + 1 = (x+1)^2 - 3x or x^{2^n} - 1 factorization) to show growth of number of prime factors or multiplicity behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 1.84 and 1.90: use factorization properties and coprimality arguments to show increase in distinct prime divisors or lower bounds on total prime factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use division algorithm + induction to construct representations from divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply division with remainder to reduce the size of the problem and use the induction hypothesis to represent quotient as sum of divisors, then lift to larger factorial or product by multiplying divisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.85: write a = b(n+1)+c with 0≤c≤n, represent b as sum of divisors of n!, then multiply by (n+1) to obtain divisors of (n+1)! and add c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct numbers with desired modular divisibility via Pigeonhole/residue argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Form several candidates differing in leading digit choices; show their residues modulo base are distinct, forcing one to be divisible by desired modulus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.91: given n-digit odd-digit numbers A1..A5 with residues 1·2^n+a,...,9·2^n+a modulo 5, these five residues exhaust classes mod5 so some Ai divisible by 5^{n+1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parity/recursive definitions to enumerate rationals uniquely
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a sequence recursively distinguishing even/odd indices (e.g., x_{2n}=1+x_n, x_{2n+1}=1/(1+x_{2n})) to generate all positive rationals exactly once and prove uniqueness by injectivity arguments on parity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.87: prove existence by induction on a+b (coprime numerator/denominator), uniqueness by showing sequence terms are pairwise distinct through parity-based descent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply combinatorial induction: enlarge sets and argue new sums are distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: When counting distinct ±-sums from ordered positive numbers, show that appending largest element creates k+1 new sums distinct from previous ones, giving recursive count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 1.88: with ordered a1<...<ak<ak+1, the k+1 sums s+ak+1 - ai are all greater than s and distinct, yielding lower bound on number of distinct sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize total length to enforce non-crossing matching in plane pairings
rubrics_metrics.description: For bipartite matching of red and blue points, choose matching minimizing total segment length; if two segments cross, swapping endpoints reduces total length (by triangle inequality), contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 2.11: pick global minimizer of total length; show any crossing segments can be uncrossed to reduce length using Problem 2.5 inequality, so minimal configuration has no crossings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reflection across midpoint to compare distances and create parallelograms
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect a point across the midpoint of a segment to obtain parallelogram relations (equal opposite vectors) and apply triangle inequality to bound differences of distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 2.6: reflect O across midpoint M to O'; parallelogram AOBO' gives OA = BO', then triangle inequality in triangle B O O' yields 2 OM > |OA - OB|, with equality conditions examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare side/diagonal sums in quadrilaterals via triangle inequality and intersection point
rubrics_metrics.description: Let O be intersection of diagonals; use AO+OB > AB and CO+OD > CD to deduce AC+BD > AB+CD and similar inequalities for other side pairings; sum or average such inequalities to compare with perimeter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 2.5: use diagonal intersection and triangle inequality to prove max(AB+CD, AD+BC) < AC+BD < AB+BC+CD+DA, and related bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare altitudes/medians sums to perimeter using right-triangle comparisons and centroid ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Show each altitude is less than corresponding side (right-triangle leg < hypotenuse); for medians use centroid divides median 2:1 to relate medians to side lengths and deduce bounds relative to perimeter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 2.7–2.9: altitudes sum < perimeter; medians sum > P/2 and < 3P/4 via centroid properties and triangle inequality (use prior problem results as needed).
